prompt: Which threat is this lesson's way of storing passwords built against?
hint: Think of who has the most time.

choices.text: Somebody with a copy of the users table, offline
choices.why: Right. They can test guesses offline for as long as they like, and none of it passes through your login code.

choices.text: A stranger trying passwords at the login route
choices.why: That one is real too, and lesson 12 limits it. Here the threat is a copy of the table, where no route is involved.

choices.text: A user who forgets their password
choices.why: Forgetting is a support problem. The storage decision is about what a leak gives away.

choices.text: Traffic read on its way between client and server
choices.why: That is what HTTPS defends, in lesson 13. A hash in the database does nothing for a password in transit.

prompt: A team encrypts every password with AES and keeps the key in the API's configuration file. A backup of the server's disk leaks. What does it give away?
hint: Where does the key live?

choices.text: Nothing, because AES has not been broken
choices.why: AES does not need breaking: the key is in the same backup, and decrypting with it is the normal use.

choices.text: Hashes that still have to be guessed one by one
choices.why: Encryption is not hashing. What is stored comes back whole with the key, with no guessing.

choices.text: Every password
choices.why: Right. The program that checks logins needs the key, so it sits with the program, and the backup takes both.

choices.text: Only the passwords of users logged in at the time
choices.why: The backup holds every stored row, logged in or not, and the key opens all of them.

prompt: Match what the column holds to what a leaked table gives away.
hint: Two of them give everything; the difference is when.

pairs.right: every password, once the key leaks too
each password at a cost per guess, per account

prompt: Why is SHA-256 the wrong function for storing passwords?
hint: Look at the first row of hashrate.py.

choices.text: Its output can be reversed with enough computing
choices.why: A hash is one-way, and nobody reverses SHA-256. Guessing and comparing is the problem, not reversal.

choices.text: It is fast
choices.why: Right. It is built to be as fast as hardware allows, which makes every guess against a leaked table cheap.

choices.text: Its 256-bit output is too short to stay unique
choices.why: 256 bits is plenty for uniqueness. Two passwords colliding is not how a leak goes wrong.

choices.text: It was broken and withdrawn as a standard
choices.why: SHA-256 is a current standard and fine for fingerprinting data. Its speed is the trouble here.

prompt: In the lesson's run, SHA-256 computed 1,101,475.6 hashes a second and bcrypt at cost 10 computed 16.0. How many times faster was SHA-256? Answer to the nearest thousand.
hint: Divide one rate by the other.

prompt: A colleague says: a graphics card would compute every row of hashrate.py thousands of times faster, so the comparison is meaningless. What is the best reply?
hint: What does a graphics card have little of per guess?

choices.text: Graphics cards cannot compute password hashes at all
choices.why: They can; they are what people use against leaked tables. The question is how much they gain.

choices.text: Python already runs as fast as any hardware can
choices.why: One Python loop on one core is far slower than dedicated hardware, as the lesson says.

choices.text: Only the SHA-256 row would get any faster on such a card
choices.why: Every row gets faster on dedicated hardware. They do not all gain by the same factor.

choices.text: The ratio carries over, and the memory-hard rows gain the least
choices.why: Right. Each guess in flight needs its own block of memory for scrypt and Argon2id, which is what such hardware is short of.

prompt: Where is a password's salt kept?
hint: It is not a secret.

choices.text: In a file outside the database that only the server can read
choices.why: That describes a pepper, which is secret and the same for every row. A salt is neither.

choices.text: Nowhere: it is worked out from the user's name each time
choices.why: A salt derived from the name is predictable, and the same on every site, which defeats its purpose.

choices.text: In the row, beside the hash
choices.why: Right. bcrypt and Argon2id even write it inside the stored string; its job is to be unique, not hidden.

choices.text: In the session cookie of the user's browser
choices.why: The server needs the salt to check a password, including from a new browser, so it keeps it.

prompt: Two rows of an unsalted SHA-256 users table hold the same hash. What does that tell whoever reads the leak?
hint: The same input always gives the same SHA-256.

choices.text: The two users chose the same password
choices.why: Right. That is a leak on its own, and one table computed in advance answers both rows.

choices.text: Nothing, until one of the hashes is reversed
choices.why: No reversal is needed: equal hashes of the same function mean equal inputs.

choices.text: The two hashes collided by chance
choices.why: A chance collision in SHA-256 is not something anybody has ever seen. Equal passwords are the explanation.

choices.text: One account was created as a copy of the other
choices.why: The hash depends on the password alone, not on how the account was made.

prompt: Which of these does a random salt per password achieve? Choose all that apply.
hint: Separate what makes rows different from what makes a guess slow.

choices.text: A table of hashes computed in advance stops working
choices.why: Right. It would need an entry for every possible salt.

choices.text: Each guess against a single row takes longer
choices.why: Salted SHA-256 still ran at more than a million a second. The cost per guess is the cost factor's job.

choices.text: Two users with one password get different hashes
choices.why: Right. The two bcrypt strings for `sunshine` showed it.

choices.text: A hash cannot be checked without a secret key
choices.why: The salt is public and sits in the row. A secret key is what a pepper adds.

prompt: bcrypt reads at most ___ bytes of a password and ignores the rest.
hint: The two passwords in the transcript agreed on that many `a`.

prompt: One bcrypt hash at cost 10 took 62.651 ms on the lab machine. About how many milliseconds would one hash at cost 13 take there?
hint: Each step of the cost doubles the work.

prompt: A user registers with a long passphrase in Portuguese, full of accented letters, on a service using Ubuntu's bcrypt 3.2.2. What happens to the part after its 72nd byte?
hint: Bytes, not characters, and this version says nothing.

choices.text: The library raises an error and registration fails
choices.why: This version does not refuse; the transcript's `True` shows the extra bytes were simply dropped.

choices.text: Nothing is lost, since the limit counts 72 letters
choices.why: The limit counts bytes, and `canção` was 6 characters and 8 bytes.

choices.text: It is ignored, silently
choices.why: Right. Anything after it can be changed and the password still verifies.

choices.text: The accented letters are replaced by question marks before hashing
choices.why: The bytes are hashed as UTF-8, accents included. The issue is how many of them are read.

prompt: To let bcrypt take long passwords, a team runs each password through plain SHA-256 first and gives the result to bcrypt. What does OWASP's sheet say about that?
hint: The sheet's formula has two more ingredients.

choices.text: It is the fix the sheet recommends, exactly as the team wrote it
choices.why: The sheet calls a plain pre-hash dangerous. Its formula keys the hash and encodes it.

choices.text: Use an HMAC with a secret key, then base64, before bcrypt
choices.why: Right: `bcrypt(base64(hmac-sha384(password, pepper)))`, with the pepper kept out of the database.

choices.text: Raise the cost to 14 instead, which lifts the limit
choices.why: The cost changes the time, not how many bytes are read; 72 stays 72 at every cost.

choices.text: Change the prefix from `$2b$` to `$2y$`
choices.why: The prefix names a version of the algorithm. No version reads more than 72 bytes.

prompt: Match each scrypt setting to what it controls.
hint: One of the right-hand descriptions is `dklen`, which is not on the left.

pairs.right: how many blocks, a power of two
the size of a block, 128 × r bytes
the memory ceiling for one call

right_distractors: how many bytes of hash come back

prompt: How many MiB does one scrypt hash need with `N=2^16` and `r=8`?
hint: 128 × r × N bytes.

prompt: Why does the lesson say `hashlib.scrypt` is the harder one to use correctly in a new system?
hint: Compare what it returns with a bcrypt string.

choices.text: It is not memory-hard, so hardware runs it cheaply
choices.why: It is the memory-hard one; the peak grew from 29 to 141 MiB with N.

choices.text: It returns bare bytes and leaves the rest to you
choices.why: Right. The salt, the parameters and the comparison are yours to handle, and each is a place for a mistake that a test with the right password never shows.

choices.text: It gives different results on two different machines
choices.why: Same password, salt and settings give the same bytes everywhere, or nothing could verify.

choices.text: It cannot be given a salt, so equal passwords collide
choices.why: It takes `salt=` as an argument; the transcript passed one.

prompt: In the string `$argon2id$v=19$m=19456,t=2,p=1$…`, the value of `m` is a quantity of memory measured in ___.
hint: 19456 of them make 19 MiB.

prompt: With `m=19456` unchanged, `p` goes from 1 to 8. What happens to the memory one hash uses?
hint: OWASP's sheet warns about reading this parameter wrong.

choices.text: It is multiplied by eight, to 152 MiB in total
choices.why: That is the misreading the sheet warns about: `p` is not a multiplier.

choices.text: It is divided by eight
choices.why: The total stays `m`; each lane gets an eighth of it, which is not the same thing.

choices.text: It doubles, since lanes come in pairs
choices.why: Lanes do not come in pairs; `m` alone sets the total.

choices.text: It stays at 19 MiB, split into eight lanes
choices.why: Right. `m` is the total, and `p` only decides how many lanes share it.

prompt: Put the steps for choosing Argon2id parameters in order.
hint: A published minimum comes first, the code last.
items: Start from OWASP's minimum, `m=19456 t=2 p=1`
Measure on a machine like the one that serves logins
Raise `m`, then `t`, until a hash takes what a login can spend
Multiply the memory by the logins expected at once
Write the result in one place and let old hashes upgrade at login
trap: Measuring on a laptop and copying the number to the server chooses for the wrong machine.

prompt: Logins use `m=65536`. The server expects 40 logins at the same moment. How many MiB do the hashes need at that moment?
hint: 65536 KiB is 64 MiB.

prompt: OWASP's sheet says its five Argon2id settings give an equal level of defence. On the lab machine they took between 28.368 and 102.377 ms. What should you conclude?
hint: Defence and time are two different measurements.

choices.text: The fastest setting is weaker and should be avoided
choices.why: The sheet rates them equal; a faster setting on one machine is not a weaker one.

choices.text: The sheet is wrong, because time is what defence means
choices.why: Memory is part of the cost too, and memory is what hardware running guesses side by side lacks.

choices.text: Equal defence is not equal time, so measure on your own server
choices.why: Right. Pick among them, or above them, by what one login can spend on the machine that runs it.

choices.text: The lab machine is faulty and its numbers can be ignored
choices.why: Different settings stress memory and passes differently; the spread is ordinary.

prompt: After `memory_cost` changed from 19456 to 47104, why did Ana's old hash still verify?
hint: Where did `verify` get `m` from?

choices.text: `check_needs_rehash` converted the old hash first
choices.why: It runs after a successful verify, and it cannot convert anything without the password.

choices.text: Argon2id ignores the memory setting when it verifies
choices.why: It uses the memory setting; it uses the stored one, `m=19456`.

choices.text: The `sed` command rewrote the stored rows too
choices.why: `sed` edited `passwords.py` and nothing in `shelf.db`.

choices.text: `verify` read the parameters from the stored string
choices.why: Right. Each row says how it was made, so old rows keep working while new ones use the new numbers.

prompt: After the parameters change in `passwords.py`, which accounts end up with hashes made the new way?
hint: The rehash needs something only a login provides.

choices.text: All of them, the next time the program starts
choices.why: Starting the program does not have anybody's password, and a hash cannot be remade without it.

choices.text: Those whose owners next log in correctly
choices.why: Right. Only then is the password in hand. An account nobody uses keeps its old hash.

choices.text: None, until a database migration rewrites them
choices.why: A migration has no passwords either. Login does the upgrade, row by row.

choices.text: Those whose owners fail a login
choices.why: A failed login has a wrong password in hand, and `login` returns before the rehash.

prompt: Put what `login` in `passwords.py` does in order, for a correct password.
hint: The rehash comes after the answer is known.
items: Look up the row for the name
Verify the password against the stored string
Ask whether the stored parameters differ from `HASHER`'s
Store a new hash if they do
trap: Checking for a rehash before verifying would rehash whatever was typed, right or wrong.

prompt: Match each piece of this lesson to what it is.
hint: Public or secret, per row or shared.

pairs.right: public, and different in every row
secret, shared by every row, kept outside the database
what an unknown name is checked against
what makes one guess take longer

right_distractors: what lets a forgotten password be read back

prompt: Which of these does NIST SP 800-63B ask of the passwords a service accepts? Choose all that apply.
hint: Length and the blocklist stayed; composition and expiry went.

choices.text: A digit, a capital letter and a symbol in each
choices.why: Composition rules are exactly what it tells services not to impose.

choices.text: At least 15 characters when it is the only factor
choices.why: Right, and 8 when it is one of two factors.

choices.text: A forced change every 90 days
choices.why: It says not to force periodic changes, only a change when there is evidence of compromise.

choices.text: Refusal of those known to be breached
choices.why: Right. A blocklist of common and breached passwords is required.

choices.text: Room for at least 64 characters
choices.why: Right: a maximum of at least 64, so passphrases fit.

prompt: In the k-anonymity check against Have I Been Pwned, what does the service receive?
hint: Count the characters in the URL.

choices.text: The whole SHA-1 of the password
choices.why: A whole hash of a common password identifies it at once. Only part of it is sent.

choices.text: The password itself, over HTTPS
choices.why: HTTPS protects the trip, not what the receiver learns. The design sends far less.

choices.text: Five hex characters
choices.why: Right: the first five of the SHA-1, shared by hundreds of passwords. Your server compares the other 35.

choices.text: The Argon2id string stored in the row
choices.why: That string is salted and unique to the row; no list could contain it.

prompt: Every stored hash depends on the pepper, so replacing it means each user has to choose a new ___.
hint: What does the user type at login?

prompt: Why does `login` check an unknown name against `DECOY`?
hint: Compare the bars in the figure.

choices.text: So a missing account takes as long as a wrong password
choices.why: Right. Without it the reply would come back in under a millisecond and give the name away.

choices.text: So that unknown names can be registered on the spot
choices.why: Nothing is registered at login; the result is `False` either way.

choices.text: To slow down users who mistype their own name
choices.why: Slowing people down is not the aim; matching the time of a wrong password is.

choices.text: To keep a spare hash ready for the next registration
choices.why: The decoy is never stored for anyone; it exists only to be checked against.

prompt: A team pastes a fixed decoy string, made with `m=19456`, into the code, and a year later raises `HASHER` to `m=262144`. What goes wrong?
hint: `verify` uses the parameters written in the string it is given.

choices.text: Unknown names answer faster than wrong passwords again
choices.why: Right. The decoy still costs a `m=19456` hash while real rows grow towards `m=262144`, so the two times drift apart.

choices.text: Every existing user is locked out
choices.why: Existing rows verify with their own stored parameters, decoy or no decoy.

choices.text: The decoy starts matching real passwords
choices.why: It is a hash of a random string, whatever its parameters.

choices.text: Nothing, since the decoy's timing does not depend on `m`
choices.why: Time grows with `m`: 40.003 ms at 19456 against 871.884 ms at 262144 in the lesson's run.

prompt: Order these by how many hashes a second the lab machine computed, fastest first.
hint: One of them is not a password hash at all.
trap: OWASP's minimums are not equal in time: scrypt's was the slowest row of the six.

prompt: What is it about a bcrypt or Argon2id hash that lets a team raise the cost later without anybody resetting a password?
hint: Old rows have to keep verifying.

choices.text: A pepper
choices.why: A pepper is the one thing that cannot change without every user resetting.

choices.text: A salt per user, stored in the row beside each hash
choices.why: The salt makes rows differ; it says nothing about which cost made them.

choices.text: A decoy hash, checked whenever a name does not exist
choices.why: The decoy hides which names exist. It plays no part in upgrading.

choices.text: The parameters written into each stored string
choices.why: Right. `verify` reads them back, each row verifies with its own, and `check_needs_rehash` upgrades it at the next correct login.

prompt: A leaked users table holds strings like `$argon2id$v=19$m=19456,t=2,p=1$…`, with no pepper. Which statements are true? Choose all that apply.
hint: The salt is in the string; the cost is per guess.

choices.text: Every guess against a row costs a full Argon2id hash
choices.why: Right: 19 MiB and two passes for every single guess.

choices.text: The salt has to be found before any guess can be tested
choices.why: The salt is the fourth field of the string, in plain sight.

choices.text: A guess tested against one row says nothing about another
choices.why: Right. Each row has its own salt, so each is its own job.

choices.text: Common passwords can be looked up in a table computed in advance
choices.why: A table computed in advance would need an entry for every salt; the per-row salt is what defeats it.

prompt: A secret HMAC ___ kept outside the database means that a leaked copy of the table, on its own, cannot test a single guess.
hint: It is what `openssl dgst -hmac` was given.
